descriptionChirho: Physical heat from the sun or the warm season, referring to the warmth of the day, the hot part of the year, or the sun's intensity. Appears in contexts describing the cycles of nature (Gen 8:22 'heat and cold'), the heat of midday (Gen 18:1, 1 Sam 11:9/11), scorching conditions for plants (Jer 17:8), and the melting power of sunlight (Job 6:17, 24:19). Multilingual glosses converge on thermal vocabulary: حَرّ (Arb), Hitze (Deu), calor (Spa), गरमी/गर्मी (Hin), 더움/더위 (Kor), chaleur (Fra), confirming the consistent meteorological-thermal sense across all these occurrences.

Figurative use of heat to describe people burning with anger, lust, or intense emotion. In Jeremiah 51:39, Babylon's people are 'heated' or inflamed (with drink or passion) before their destruction. The Korean gloss 달아올랐을 때에 ('when they became heated/inflamed') and English 'when they are heated' explicitly mark the metaphorical transfer from physical temperature to emotional state. This figurative extension is a recognized sense in Hebrew lexicography (BDB), distinct from literal atmospheric or bodily heat.

Describing an object or substance as physically hot in temperature, as in heated bread or food. In Joshua 9:12 (ref 9:21:7), the Gibeonites describe bread that was hot when they took it. The multilingual glosses use adjectival forms: حَارّ (Arb), hot (Deu/Eng/Fra), caliente (Spa), गरम (Hin), 뜨거운 (Kor), all indicating a predicate adjective of temperature rather than a noun of atmospheric heat, distinguishing this from the meteorological sense.

Physical warmth needed for the human body, the comfort of being warm rather than cold, especially in the context of seeking shelter or coverings. In 1 Kings 1:6 (ref 37:1:6 = Haggai context), the concern is for bodily warmth. Arabic لِلدِّفْءِ ('for warmth'), Hindi गर्माहट ('warmth'), Korean 따뜻함 ('warmth'), and Spanish calor all point to the sense of thermal comfort for the body rather than solar or atmospheric heat, making this a distinct semantic usage.
